references.text: In the preceding verse, Jesus rebukes the crowd because they can interpret the signs of earth and sky but cannot judge the present time. [ref:Luk 12:56|Luke 12:56] forms the immediate context for the call to judge for oneself what is right.

Paul urges the Corinthians to judge for themselves: "Judge for yourselves!" ([ref:1 Kor 11:13|1 Corinthians 11:13]). The same principle of using one's own judgment to decide what is right applies here.

Paul says: "I speak as to sensible people. Judge for yourselves what I say!" ([ref:1 Kor 10:15|1 Corinthians 10:15]). Here Paul appeals to his listeners' own ability to judge what is right, just as Jesus does in Luke 12:57.

Jesus says: "Do not judge by appearances, but judge with righteous judgment!" ([ref:Joh 7:24|John 7:24]). Here Jesus calls for righteous judgment (τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν), reflecting the words τὸ δίκαιον and κρίνετε in Luke 12:57.
Moses commands judges to judge fairly among their brothers ([ref:5 Mos 1:16|Deuteronomy 1:16]). The principle of judging what is right is fundamental in Old Testament legal practice.

"Appoint judges and officials ... they shall judge the people with righteous judgments" ([ref:5 Mos 16:18|Deuteronomy 16:18]). The Hebrew ideal of righteous judgment (מִשְׁפַּט־צֶדֶק) underlies Jesus' call to judge what is right.

Jesus says that when the disciples see the signs, they should "by themselves" understand that God's kingdom is near ([ref:Luk 21:30-31|Luke 21:30-31]). The same expectation that people should be able to assess the situation based on their own insight and observation.

In [ref:Matt 5:25|Matthew 5:25], Jesus urges reconciliation with one's opponent while still on the way, which corresponds to the parallel passage in [ref:Luk 12:58|Luke 12:58] that follows directly after this verse. The call to judge what is right leads into a practical application.
